blocks.content: UML stands for Unified Modeling Language. It is a standard way to draw out the structure of a software system before or after you build it.
Out of all the diagrams UML offers, class diagrams are the most commonly used one.
A class diagram shows you a bird's eye view of your system what classes exist, what data they hold, what they can do, and how they relate to each other.

In this article we will cover the core building blocks of a class diagram, how to read and draw each one, the types of relationships classes can have, and simple real-world examples to make it all click.
1. Anatomy of a Class
Every class diagram starts with a class. UML draws it as a box chopped into three horizontal sections name on top, data in the middle, actions at the bottom.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245788648-278e9f90.png
Let's walk through each piece.
Name Section (top) Just the class name written in PascalCase. Think of it as the label on the box it tells you what kind of object this represents.
Data Section (middle) The information the class keeps track of. Each line follows this pattern:
["visibility name: type"]
So -email: String is a private field named email that holds text. The - in front means nothing outside this class can directly read or change it.
Want to be more specific? You can also write:
["visibility name: type [multiplicity] = defaultValue"]
Something like -scores: List [0..*] tells you the field can hold any number of items from zero upwards.
Actions Section (bottom) The things an object of this class is capable of doing. Each line looks like:
["visibility name(parameters): returnType"]
So +greet(): void is a public action called greet that takes no input and gives nothing back. And +setEmail(email: String): voidtakes a piece of text as input and returns nothing.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245788765-a46802c5.jpg
2. Special Class Types
Not every box in a class diagram is a plain class. Some define contracts, some are partially built, and some just hold a fixed list of values. Each one has its own UML notation.
Interfaces
A class diagram is not just plain classes. Some building blocks define rules, some are partially complete, and some simply lock down a list of fixed options. Here is how each one looks in UML.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245788969-4dbd4769.png
Any class that connects to Trackable with a dashed arrow is signing up to deliver every method written inside it. No exceptions.
Abstract Classes
An abstract class is a blueprint that is only partially filled in. Some methods come ready to use, others are left blank on purpose for child classes to complete. The <> tag marks it at the top.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245789053-8219a8b6.png

calculateBonus() and generatePayslip() are abstract every type of employee computes these differently so they are left for subclasses to fill in. getName() is the same for everyone so it is implemented once right here.
Pick an abstract class when child classes share real data or common behavior. Pick an interface when completely unrelated classes just need to follow the same set of rules.
Enumerations
An enumeration pins down a fixed collection of named values. The <> tag identifies it and the possible values are listed in the body.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245789140-6e72d539.png

Use an enum whenever something can only ever be one of a known set of options. A traffic light is always RED, YELLOW, or GREEN never something else. Hardcoding these as plain text strings is asking for typos and bugs. An enum keeps the options locked and safe.
3. Relationships
The lines between classes are where a diagram really comes to life. UML gives you six types of relationships, each carrying a different level of connection and dependency.
1. Dependency loosest connection
One class briefly reaches into another to get something done maybe as a method argument or a temporary local variable. Nothing is stored. Once the method call ends the connection vanishes.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245789297-cac397f8.png
The dashed arrow is the UML symbol for dependency. NotificationService borrows EmailClient for one operation and then lets it go. It never keeps it around as a field.
Use it when: class A needs class B only inside a single method and stores nothing afterward.
2. Association
One class holds onto another as a permanent field. The bond outlasts any single method call. Each object has its own lifespan and neither depends on the other to exist.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245789387-c5cb0d45.png
The solid arrow is the UML symbol for association. Doctor keeps a list of Patient objects as a field. If a patient is removed the doctor still exists, and the other way around too.
Use it when: class A keeps a reference to class B as a field and both live independently.
3. Aggregation
A has-a relationship where the container holds the parts but does not own them. The parts were brought in from outside and can outlive the container or even belong to several containers at once.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245789467-9e3d4c6f.png
The hollow diamond on Library is the UML symbol for aggregation. Close the library and the books still exist they can move to another library or sit in storage. They were never exclusively owned.
Use it when: one class groups others together but the grouped objects have their own independent existence.
4. Composition
A has-a relationship where the container fully owns the parts. The parts are born inside the container and cease to exist the moment the container is destroyed. They have no life outside it.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245789624-7204807a.png

The filled diamond is the UML symbol for composition. An InvoiceItem is created inside Invoice and belongs to it completely. Delete the invoice and every item on it disappears with it. An item on its own means nothing.
Use it when: the part exists purely to serve the whole and has no purpose or identity on its own.
5. Inheritance
A is-a relationship. The child class absorbs everything the parent has all its fields and methods and is free to add more or override what it inherited.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245789791-2635c974.png

The solid line with a hollow triangle pointing at the parent is the UML symbol for inheritance. Both PushNotification and EmailNotification inherit title, message, and getTitle(). Each overrides send() in its own way and brings its own extra behavior.
Use it when: a real is-a relationship exists and the child genuinely needs the parent's data and behavior. If it feels like a stretch, composition is probably the better call.
6. Realization
The bond between an interface and the class that fulfills it. The class is making a binding commitment to implement every single method the interface declares.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245789914-60a84497.png

The dashed line with a hollow triangle pointing at the interface is the UML symbol for realization. SalesReport and InventoryReport share no parent class and have nothing in common structurally but both honor the Exportable contract and deliver their own version of each method.

Inheritance vs Realization: Inheritance hands you actual working code from a parent. Realization hands you a set of rules to follow and trusts you to write the code yourself. Solid line for inheritance, dashed line for realization.

blocks.content: Relationship Strength Spectrum
All six relationships sit on a scale from loosest to tightest coupling. Worth knowing by heart it comes up constantly in design discussions and interviews.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245790032-f4f561e3.png

The guiding principle: always reach for the weakest relationship that gets the job done. If you do not need a stored reference, a dependency beats an association. If the part can live on its own, aggregation beats composition. Looser coupling means your code bends without breaking.
4. Combined Example: Hospital Management System
Let's pull everything together with a real scenario. Design the core model for a hospital system patients, doctors, appointments, prescriptions and billing.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1778245790141-b74f4500.png
Let's trace through every relationship in the diagram:
Composition

Appointment owns Prescription Prescriptions are written during an appointment and belong entirely to it. They are created inside the appointment, have no meaning without it, and disappear when it is deleted. Filled diamond on Appointment.
Association

Patient and Doctor to Appointment Both hold a persistent reference to appointments as fields. But a patient does not stop existing when an appointment is cancelled, and neither does the doctor. Both sides live independently.
Dependency
Appointment uses Payable During billing, Appointment calls methods on a Payable object but never stores it as a field. The connection exists only inside that one operation and then disappears.
Realization

CashPayment and InsurancePayment implement Payable The two payment handlers share no parent class and work completely differently under the hood but both honor the Payable contract and deliver their own version of charge()and issueRefund().
Enumeration

Appointment uses AppointmentStatus Every appointment is always in exactly one of four known states. Representing that as free text would be fragile. An enum locks the options down and makes invalid states impossible.
